highlights.title: Silicon Valley Doesn't Get Why You Hate AI
highlights.summary: Technology leaders don’t seem to understand society’s gripes about AI, but boy, are they posting through it.
body: Silicon Valley is trying to make sense of the growing backlash against artificial intelligence, but so far, it’s not going that well. The inconvenient truth is that a significant portion of the world is not optimistic about the technology they’re building. But recent attempts to diagnose the root of the problem by CEOs like Meta’s Mark Zuckerberg and Anthropic’s Dario Amodei indicate they don’t understand what’s actually driving society’s disdain for AI.

The rest of popular culture, meanwhile, is finding ways to capitalize on AI hate. Just look at this new commercial for Liquid Death and Garage Beer. The two beverage brands teamed up with former Philadelphia Eagles football player and Taylor Swift brother-in-law Jason Kelce, who invited people to pee in bottles and send them to AI data centers. In an interview with Marketing Dive, Liquid Death’s creative lead said the data center backlash was “literally the one thing that unites all Americans right now.”

highlights.title: Why a German football superstar is now playing in the third tier
highlights.summary: "Not normal." It is a phrase that Alexandra Popp turns to more than once when speaking after her debut for Borussia Dortmund. She has scored twice. The team has won 3-0. Nothing unusual there. But the crowd of 4,572 in Germany's third tier is new.
body: Alexandra Popp scored twice on her debut for Borussia Dortmund in their 3-0 win over Arminia Bielefeld. Adam Bate was there to see it and speak to the German legend about walking away from top-level football to join the third division club she supported as a girl...

Popp is already a phenomenon here. The average attendance at Dortmund last season was below half the number at the atmospheric Stadion Rote Erde for this game against Arminia Bielefeld. Season ticket sales have almost tripled from 600 to 1700.

It is because Popp has come. This summer, the former captain of the Germany national team with 67 international goals to her name joined the club she supported as a girl. It is a homecoming that has captured the imagination among her fellow fans.

Her shirt is everywhere in Dortmund and not just among the growing fanbase for the women's team. Sales of the shirt that bears her name are currently outselling those of Serhou Guirassy, the top scorer for the men's team for each of the past two seasons.

highlights.title: 65 Years Later, the Best "Peanuts' Linus Quote Is Still an All-Time Great Comic Strip Moment
highlights.summary: This got a little watered down as the strip continued, and Linus isn’t quite as intellectual in the various cartoon adaptations (his Bible monologue in A Charlie Brown Christmas notwithstanding), but he has a theologian's knowledge of the Bible and can pontificate like a Ph.D. in philosophy.
body: You can generally map most of the main characters in Charles Schulz's Peanuts onto a sort of body/brain model. Snoopy is the strip's imagination. Charlie Brown is its undiagnosed anxiety. Lucy Van Pelt is a stand-in for the specific rage of being a little kid in a world that was made for adults. If you accept that premise, then Linus Van Pelt is the brains of the operation.

Peanuts ran for just under 50 years. While Linus wasn't part of the core cast until 1952 (two years into the strip's existence) and didn't start talking until 1954, he quickly became one of the central characters. As a result, if you're looking to put together a top 10 or 15 or 20 list of Linus's best lines, you're somewhat spoiled for choice. It'd almost be easier to group them by topic, like how a few Peanuts collections are arranged by specific themes.

If you had to simply pick one, though, my choice is from relatively early in Peanuts' run, on April 26, 1961. It's not quite a political cartoon, but it's one of the few examples of Peanuts getting close enough to one to count.

In those first 720 seconds we meet Thibaut (Benjamin Lavernhe), a well-heeled classical music conductor in Paris, who discovers that he will need to find a blood marrow transplant as he…
body: Belatedly opening Stateside after proving a domestic hit in 2024, Emmanuel Courcol's film succumbs to formula, but is lifted by its precise construction and strong lead performances.

Lottin is particularly intelligent in articulating Jimmy’s shame at his lack of means and achievement, inflected with pride and a lightly worn resentment that comes out in bursts of passive-aggressive joshing; meanwhile, Lavernhe deftly portrays the well-meaning and likable Thibaut as, conversely, insufficiently ashamed of his good fortune, at least early on: This smooth Parisian bobo does not even perceive how he flaunts his wealth and education.

In parallel, “The Marching Band” depicts a working-class community struggling with poverty and unemployment, for whom the musical collective — in which Jimmy plays the trombone, alongside his on-off girlfriend Sabrina (Sarah Suco) — has become a lifeline. Thibaut becomes involved, but will he be able to save the band from ruin? Here, the film closely mirrors the 1996 British comedy “Brassed Off,” making it a dead cert that we’ll eventually get a barn-burning finale showing the federating power of music in adversity.

highlights.title: Why dodgy doors are the latest casualty of the UK heatwaves
highlights.summary: Sticking or unlockable doors are yet another problem caused by the hot summer, but winter can also bring difficulties. Thursday was another busy day for Alan Hickman, a Bournemouth-based locksmith who works in the area around the New Forest (“though I’m currently dodging the bit between Ringwood…
body: Speaking on his way to see a man who can’t close his patio doors – “probably because they’ve got some expansion issues” – he then has a callout to see an elderly woman who needs a lockbox installed for her carer, before visiting a customer in Westbourne “to sort another composite door that can’t lock”.

Such cases of sticking, unopenable or unlockable doors are much more common at the moment, says Hickman, due, like so much else, to the very hot weather across much of the UK over the past few months.

“We’re getting what feels like double the amount of calls a day because customers’ doors just aren’t able to open, or they can’t close them at the end of a hot day until they’ve cooled down again,” he says. Hickman has worked with LockRite, one of the UK’s largest networks of uniformed locksmiths, for 14 years but this summer has “definitely brought a significant increase” in heat-related callouts.

highlights.title: Paving the way for greener ammonia production
highlights.summary: New MIT research could lead to better materials for a fossil-fuel-free process for making the chemical that's essential to fertilizer and other products.
body: Ammonia is one of the most important chemicals produced in the world, ranking second only to sulfuric acid in the total volume produced each year. It is used mostly to make fertilizer, which is essential to feeding the world’s population. Yet its production accounts for up to 2 percent of the world’s energy consumption and about 1.5 percent of greenhouse gas emissions, so the search has been underway for ways to produce ammonia more sustainably.

The traditional way of making ammonia, in use for more than a century and accounting for the vast majority of production, is the Haber-Bosch process, which relies on fossil fuels to provide the needed heat. Hydrogen used in the process is also largely produced from fossil fuels.
There is another way, using electrochemistry instead of heat and pressure, but so far this method has not been anywhere near economically competitive at the scales needed.

highlights.title: 5 Nintendo Games You Need to Play at Least Once
highlights.summary: Nintendo 's reputation for decades of certified bangers is well-earned, though between new releases and the classics that hog all the attention, it's easy to overlook some of the company's more influential games.
body: I'm not gonna tell you to go play Super Mario Bros. 3 or A Link to the Past. You should play them, but you've probably heard that from a dozen other people already. This list is more interested in examining a few pivotal games from Nintendo's history that marked turning points for the company, either for the risk involved in making them or by representing a high point in creative design that informed Nintendo's future strategies. All of these are available in some form or another on modern hardware, either via remakes, Nintendo Switch Online 's retro library, or even on PC thanks to later ports.

Nintendo played it safe with the GameCube. You might think otherwise, what with Mario Sunshine sending the plumber on a goop-cleaning vacation and The Wind Waker turning Link and Zelda into cartoons. These were still Mario and Zelda games, though. And what is Luigi's Mansion, but a Mario is Missing that doesn't suck? Pikmin was something new and wildly different than anything Nintendo had developed for years: A real-time strategy game (a genre that, nearly three decades later, remains quite niche) starring a corporate lackey and an army of sentient, expendable vegetables.

highlights.title: ‘Good People’ Review: Milcho Manchevski’s Haunting Documentary Revisits the Kočani Nightclub Fire Through Survivors’ Eyes
highlights.summary: On March 16, 2025, a fire broke out at the Pulse nightclub in the small North Macedonian town of Kočani, injuring hundreds and killing 63 people due to burn damage, smoke inhalation and other physical traumas sustained while attendees scrambled to flee through the venue’s sole exit.
body: World premiering in competition at Sarajevo, the Golden Lion-winner’s self-funded requiem is a strikingly spare and harrowing portrait of social collapse.

But unlike those long take-heavy films, “Good People” cuts frequently between its subjects, a chorus-like effect that is sometimes choppy as editor Mishko Chunikhin flits between longer memories and observations as short as a few words. The doc starts out by describing the club’s downward spiral, with survivors — some of whose burn marks you can observe on their necks and hands — sharing eerily similar experiences. The beginning of the fire was widely mistaken as a special effect put on by the pop group performing at the time, and the flames spread quicker than clubbers could realize what was happening.

highlights.summary: As the couple plans their return to the UK, Montecito’s whirlwind stint on the global stage may be coming to an end. The bucolic coastal California town of Montecito was thrust into the limelight six years ago as the backdrop for the Duke and Duchess of Sussex’s second act following an acrimonious…
body: But as the couple plans their return to the United Kingdom, Montecito’s whirlwind stint on the global stage may be coming to an end.

To be clear, the well-to-do enclave near Santa Barbara is unlikely to lose its reputation as a hideout for celebrities – a respite from the paparazzi den that Los Angeles, about 90 miles (145km) south, can be. Oprah, Gwyneth Paltrow and Ellen DeGeneres, among other public figures, have all resided in the tony community.

Prince Harry and Meghan, though, were arguably top contenders for Montecito’s most attention-grabbing residents. After news emerged that the couple had bought a $14.7m estate in the area, news helicopters and photographers swarmed in, to the annoyance of some neighbors.

Reporters even clamored for intel on a local Facebook page, prompting a moderator to warn journalists in a 2020 post: “No one will sell out or talk to the press. We don’t care who you are or where you came from, if you are our neighbor and act like a neighbor we support you.”

highlights.title: The Single English County Saying No to Palantir
highlights.summary: The UK government is facing calls to cancel a sprawling health care contract with Palantir. The region of Greater Manchester insists it can do a better job itself.
body: The UK government has six months to decide whether to terminate a deal worth more than $400 million between the country’s National Health Service and American software company Palantir. If one part of the NHS is already doing without Palantir, politicians are asking, why can’t the rest of the country?

In 2023, the UK commissioned Palantir to develop a “ federated data platform ” (FDP) that could ingest and organize the tangle of health data produced across the country. According to Palantir and the NHS, the new system is already cutting wait times and the length of hospital stays, and maximizing the use of operating theatres.

But lately, as Palantir technology is deployed in theatres of war and the US administration’s immigration crackdown, its deal with the NHS has become a flashpoint in the UK, drawing protests, petitions, parliamentary inquiries, and a reported rebellion among NHS workers. Other European nations, increasingly at loggerheads with the Trump administration, are also reevaluating their relationships with Palantir in a bid to minimize their dependence on US-made technology.
points: The UK government is facing calls to cancel a sprawling health care contract with Palantir.

highlights.title: AI data startup Micro1 reaches $500M gross run rate amid AI training boom
highlights.summary: Surging demand for AI training data is driving rapid growth for the startup and its rivals.
body: The near-bottomless demand for unique AI training data from top labs and corporations is driving a massive boom for a cohort of data-labeling startups.

One of these fast-growing businesses is Micro1, a four-year-old startup that expanded its gross annual run rate from $100 million to $500 million over the past eight months, according to a person familiar with the company. Like its peers that hire domain experts such as doctors, lawyers, and scientists on a contract basis, Micro1 retains roughly 60% to 70% of that figure, putting its net annual run rate between $150 million and $200 million.

While Micro1 still lags competitors like Mercor (which hit $2 billion in gross annualized revenue this summer) and Handshake (which reached $1 billion earlier this year), the startup’s revenue growth shows that there is more than enough demand to support multiple players supplying AI training data.
The rapid growth is bound to continue, with some researchers hypothesizing that future AI spending on data could rival spending on compute.

highlights.title: 5 Classic Anime That Will Never Need Remakes
highlights.summary: That said, some classic anime should never be remade. One-of-a-kind entries like Paranoia Agent (2004) and Revolutionary Girl Utena (1997) feel timeless, and the unique circumstances that helped shape these shows can never be replicated.
body: In the age of remakes and reboots, it makes sense for most classic anime to get a do-over. Think Fullmetal Alchemist: Brotherhood (2009), Hunter x Hunter (2011), or Hellsing Ultimate (2006) — these remakes are now considered definitive as they hew closer to the source material. Of course, a newer adaptation doesn’t render older ones obsolete, especially in the case of acclaimed classics like Naruto or Dragon Ball, which will forever be adored in spite of their flaws.
Although most stories benefit from a fresh take or a new style of animation, here are five classic anime that should never, ever get remakes.

highlights.title: Clash Royale research finds 85% of rage quitters enjoy gaming more after returning
highlights.summary: Supercell has revealed that 85.1% of rage quitters say they enjoy gaming more when they come back. That's according to research commissioned by Clash Royale, which surveyed 9,000 gamers across seven markets as the mobile game searches for a player to become its first-ever rage emote.... [ MORE ]
body: The research found that Mexico had the highest share of players who enjoyed the game more after returning from a rage quit, at 90.5%, while Germany recorded the lowest at 74.4%.

Globally, gamers said they rage quit because they want to do well (31.1%), care about the game (22.1%) and want to protect a winning streak (21.9%). Brazil had the highest share of gamers who had rage quit, at 77%, compared with 59% in Mexico.

The research also found that close to four in 10 gamers who rage quit have done so somewhere public. The US was the only market where gamers wanted an audience, with 55.6% of US rage quitters saying they would happily post a clip of the moment.
In the UK, 31.5% of public rage quitters had done so in a pub, while British gamers also led in ranting to a friend at 20.8% and screaming into a pillow at 17.2%.

highlights.title: ‘If I’m spending that kind of money, the shoe has to do everything’ – the backlash to the three figure trainer
highlights.summary: From Nike’s infamous 110s to £250 and back again, sneakerheads are rediscovering why cheaper shoes can be worth just as much hype as much more expensive ones. • Don’t get Fashion Statement delivered to your inbox? Sign up here.
body: When Nike’s Air Max 95 trainers first landed in Britain back in the mid-1990s, they looked unlike anything else. Created by footwear designer Sergio Lozano, the shoe had wavy layers running down its sides, neon yellow accents, and visible ‘Air’ bubbles underfoot. But in the UK, one detail quickly became as famous as the shoe itself: its £110 price tag.

The Air Max 95 immediately picked up the nickname “110” because spending £110 on trainers seemed outrageous at the time. Owning a pair quickly became a status symbol among young men across Britain, while in celebrity circles they were worn by everyone from Jay-Z to Kylie Minogue.

Over 30 years later, £110 looks relatively modest next to the upper end of the market catering to trainer enthusiasts. In a pretty neat example of trainerflation, flagship running shoes from Nike, New Balance, and Adidas easily retail for between £200 and £250.

highlights.title: OpenAI is gaining on Anthropic with business users, new data indicates
highlights.summary: Businesses are willing to flop back and forth as each lab releases new models, volatility that should give both companies' investors pause about how "sticky" enterprise AI spending really is.
body: Until both OpenAI and Anthropic get close enough to their planned IPOs to release their financials, we have to look to other sources for signs of how well their businesses are doing. One of those sources, Ramp, the corporate credit card and expense management company, has just released some surprising new data: OpenAI has started gaining on Anthropic with U.S. businesses.

OpenAI, which was once the runaway leader with both businesses and consumers, lost the lead among Ramp’s paying business users back in May. That’s when Anthropic hit 41% market share to OpenAI’s 39%. The ChatGPT maker has never regained that lead. As of July, Anthropic has nearly 44% to OpenAI’s nearly 40%.

The data covers more than 70,000 American businesses that spend billions via Ramp’s bill pay and corporate card products. Ramp’s customers are spread across industries but, as a popular Silicon Valley corporate credit card, they do skew toward the tech industry.

highlights.summary: Free from a big brand’s audience expectations, new studio GPTrack50 has created a wacky action-packed romp through a monster-filled world for its first game. Love is blind.
body: Love is blind. In Stupid Never Dies, it is also frozen solid and technically dead as Davy, the weakest zombie in monster society, discovers Julia’s body in a shopping centre and falls in love at first sight. He wants to bring her back to life and take her on a date. Unfortunately, that means defeating the King of Monsters (KOM) and accidentally saving humanity along the way.

This is the gloriously ridiculous setup for this forthcoming action RPG from GPTrack50, a new studio founded by former Capcom producer Hiroyuki Kobayashi. Its world looks much like ours, except that monsters have always been part of everyday life: whereas we might find a bear in the mountains or a stray dog in the woods, residents here encounter werewolves and zombies.

That uneasy normality ends when KOM crushes civilisation and leaves only 2% of humanity alive. Davy begins even lower down the social ladder. Zombies, says Kobayashi, are “the weakest of the weak”. But eating a mysterious egg gives this particularly unimpressive corpse the power to fight back.

highlights.title: I’ll admit it: I’ve cycled through red lights. But Britain’s traffic laws are to blame, not me | Simon Jenkins
highlights.summary: The essence of cycling is to keep moving, but London’s chaotic roads often make this difficult. My solution: fewer, not more rules. I plead guilty. I have loved and used the streets of London all my life, as a cyclist, driver and pedestrian.
body: When I try to drive at the authorised speed of 20mph on many through roads, I am hooted at and overtaken by vans, cars, coaches and buses. And when I sit dutifully on my bike at a traffic light, I am jostled by swarms of cyclists riding through on red, furious at being treated as if they were car drivers.
As for pedestrians, walking on many pavements is like taking a ride on the dodgems. Riders of ebikes and e-scooters ignore bans and expect everyone to move out of the way.

I normally approve of anarchy. There is too much regulation everywhere. The great Dutch traffic engineer Hans Monderman boldly advocated “shared space” in cities. He wanted kerbs, road markings and traffic signals minimised and replaced by “human discipline”. All road users should navigate urban space by watching out for each other all the time. Monderman is virtually unknown in Britain, but principles similar to his were trialled with success in London’s Exhibition Road and Seven Dials. His counterintuitive ideas have been applied with remarkable success across northern Europe, with accidents falling. In 2023, 45% of Copenhageners cycled to work or school.

body: The Manta launches on Kickstarter today with a focus on tailoring the controller’s functionality and feel for each game.

The Genki Manta is launching today through a Kickstarter crowdfunding campaign. The earliest backers can preorder the controller discounted to $189, while full retail pricing is expected to be $279. This is the company’s ninth crowdfunded device so while there’s always some risk with backing a Kickstarter, Genki has an excellent track record of delivering products this way.

While companies like Anbernic already have controllers with integrated screens, the Manta offers an especially deep level of customization through a settings interface powered by a dedicated Raspberry Pi RP2350 microcontroller. Players can configure and switch between multiple console, game, and user profiles, adjust thumbstick response and dead zones, increase the intensity of the haptic feedback, remap buttons, and record, edit, and combine multiple button presses to create custom macros.

The benefits of doing this, OpenAI argues, are numerous. Users can use the plug-in to sort, analyze, or edit their messages directly from ChatGPT. The plug-in also works with Codex and ChatGPT Work, so users can use it professionally, not just personally.
A brief commercial advertising the new plug-in shows a user asking the chatbot to suggest follow-up messages to their contacts based on the messages received the previous day.
You can also ask ChatGPT to delete messages for you, draft and send messages on your behalf, or search for information buried deep in your message history.

body: An English-language trailer for the critically-acclaimed anime’s second season has hit the internet to kick off Anime NYC. We finally get to hear Clancy Brown ( Detroit: Become Human, Avatar the Last Airbender ) as Weak Kingsley, a veteran Edgerunner who we see fall into the throes of cyberpsychosis and blast some chooms with his pistol. You know, typical Cyberpunk stuff.

We also get a glimpse of him taking an assignment from a concerned mother in a diner, who mentions her daughter, as well as a shot of him sitting by Talia Yang as she lies in a hospital bed. “Losing yourself… that’s worse than death,” Kingsley says in a voiceover.

D, a Snake Nation nomad, also gets some time to shine; we see him slotting a datashard into his neck as a voiceover says: “Those burns… I didn’t know anyone else survived. You’ve been out for blood? All this time?”

A burning campsite flashes across the screen, along with clips of the usual Night City ultraviolence. We see a shot of Talia in the rain, then D and Roman Carax standing by a burning corpse at night in the desert. Something crazy is happening with D’s hair here as Roman says in a voiceover: “You’re a weapon? A weapon made out of people?”

highlights.title: It’s Greg Brockman’s OpenAI now
highlights.summary: OpenAI has had a hell of a year. The company spent months battling former cofounder Elon Musk in a sensational jury trial, was hit with a high-profile trade secrets lawsuit from Apple, and faced widespread scrutiny after an unreleased model hacked another AI company.
body: Sam Altman is still CEO, but in day-to-day operations, his second-in-command is running the show.

Brockman is currently OpenAI’s president and cofounder. He’s helped lead OpenAI since its inception, described as an “engineering workhorse that pushed to build scaled-up systems that would train the AI and make it work” during the company’s early days. He’s also been ambitious from the start, famously musing in a personal journal in 2017, “Financially what will take me to $1B?” (His current stake in OpenAI is worth nearly 30 times that.) But at that point he shared power with a handful of cofounders, like chief scientist Ilya Sutskever and CEO Sam Altman.

Now, though Brockman’s title hasn’t changed in years, his purview and job description have expanded significantly. He’s essentially now second-in-command at the company — and, when it comes to day-to-day operations, the big boss.

Several of these departures — like those of Rouch, Peebles, and Weil — didn’t seem to directly affect Brockman’s position. But others expanded his authority. When Simo went on medical leave, Brockman took charge of all things product, including leading OpenAI’s super app efforts.

body: Three months after the game's relaunch, Supercell said the latest data shows its gameplay loop “quickly gets stale” for most players, causing them to drop off.
However, players who remain are spending unusually long periods in the game, the studio claims, suggesting Mo.co currently works well for a niche audience but is not ready to scale.

“Now, this won’t be fixed with small changes," said Supercell in a post. “We’re already prototyping and testing big and exciting stuff. With that being said, all the effort being relocated into developing and iterating those new features will come at an unfortunate yet unavoidable cost.
“Team members who usually dedicate their time to building all-new seasonal events, monsters, and weapons will now focus on developing those much-needed changes."

highlights.summary: A jury last month cleared the YouTuber of several sexual assault offences, but it couldn't reach a decision on three others,
body: British rapper Yung Filly will face a retrial on three rape charges in Australia, after a jury cleared him of several sexual assault offences but could not reach a decision on others.
The YouTuber, whose real name is Andres Felipe Valencia Barrientos, was charged with repeatedly raping and assaulting a fan after performing at a nightclub in Perth in 2024.
He denied all 10 charges, and last month a jury found him not guilty on three counts of rape.
He was also acquitted of one assault charge and another of strangulation, but was found guilty of two counts of assault, for which he'll be sentenced after his retrial.

highlights.title: The Business of Katseye
highlights.summary: As the world’s first multi-ethnic, English-language group modeled on the K-pop framework, Katseye has broken significant industry barriers. Their continued high-profile activities indicate their ability to adapt despite recent controversy. But can their influence be sustained?
body: Three years ago, six young women — Sophia, Lara, Manon, Daniela, Megan and Yoonchae — were catapulted into instant global fame when they appeared on the Netflix reality show, The Debut: Dream Academy, beating 100,000 other contestants to be part of the pop group Katseye.

The premise was unusual. Formed through a joint venture between the South Korean music powerhouse Hybe and American record label Geffen Records, Katseye pioneered a unique cross-market model that applied Korea’s notorious idol bootcamp infrastructure with Western mainstream pop production. Their unique heritage was an added draw — the six members come from diverse countries including the US, Switzerland, the Philippines, and South Korea.

Also crucial to the group’s image-building was the insider fashion knowledge procured from close collaborators including creative director Humberto Leon, co-founder of the once-cult shopping destination Opening Ceremony and former co-designer at Kenzo, alongside stylist Katie Qian, whose clients include Tyla, Conan Gray, Camila Cabello, and Tinashe.
In an age where fame feels more accessible than ever, only a select few manage to break through the noise. Here’s what sets them apart.
points: As the world’s first multi-ethnic, English-language group modeled on the K-pop framework, Katseye has broken significant industry barriers.
Their continued high-profile activities indicate their ability to adapt despite recent controversy.
